description.narrative: ADF is a grant mechanism supporting the Asian Development Bank’s ADB’s poorest members, including nine Pacific Island countries. Australia pushed to increase the share of ADF that goes into our region, and our advocacy achieved significant grants and technical assistance to vulnerable Pacific Island countries. Australia was the second largest donor to ADF13 through the replenishment of the Asian Development Fund (ADF). Australia’s own contribution of AUD423 million demonstrates our commitment to supporting the region’s most vulnerable in partnership with ADB as an institution with finance and expertise at scale.

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative: Approximately 597,512 people benefited from strengthened climate and disaster resilience due to reduced flooding exposure. The project's impact is evident in the enhanced resilience of the population, achieved through significant reductions in flood and drought damage costs. The subproject improved community livelihood resilience and sustainability by: ‍ 1. Avoiding Flood Damage: Mitigation measures effectively prevented flood-related losses. ‍ 2. Increasing Agricultural Productivity and Incomes: Improved irrigation management and water availability boosted agricultural output and farmers' earnings. ‍3. Enhancing Access: Upgraded rural roads and canals facilitated better access to essential services and markets. ‍ These initiatives collectively contributed to a more resilient and sustainable community.

Floods can be beneficial by bringing in plant nutrients, but severe ones devastate agricultural lands and destroy public and private property. Droughts, on the other hand, disrupt farmers' livelihoods and food supply chains. Both severe floods and droughts disproportionately affect poor and vulnerable communities, reducing incomes and increasing food insecurity. This project aims to mitigate flood and drought risks by enhancing information systems and building capacity for community-based disaster risk management (CBDRM). It includes investments in flood control embankments, and irrigation, and drainage structures in Lao PDR and Viet Nam.

In Cambodia, two collaboration agreements were achieved, including between MOU with University of California, Davis and RUA; and MOU with the Kansas State University to exchange technology on food science and other academic information. In Lao PDR, 40 bilateral meetings were held with GMS counterparts, comprising 17 bilateral working groups conducted on plant health to exchange pest lists, reports and outbreak control; 15 bilateral working group meetings conducted on animal health to discuss and agree on TAD control measures along borders and improve technical collaboration; and 12 bilateral working groups conducted on food safety to facilitate cooperation and trade and information sharing on surveillance activities. In the Lao PDR, three institutional twinning arrangements were finalised.

Isolation and quarantine facilities were established at Vila Central and Northern Provincial Hospitals, including spaces for clinicians. Infection control measures and laboratory testing capabilities were implemented, with routine self-assessments published in COVID-19 Situation Reports. Both hospitals developed capacity for managing suspected or confirmed COVID-19 cases. At least 40 public health officers or healthcare workers (40% women) improved their skills in preventing and controlling infectious diseases. All frontline staff at both hospitals (259 women and 218 men) received training in COVID-19 management and infection control in 2020. The $6 million Health Sector Preparedness and Response Plan allocated funds for infrastructure (20%), clinical management (40%), coordination and prevention (23%), and early detection and isolation (17%). This enabled an effective pandemic response, with Vanuatu maintaining no community transmission of COVID-19 until the Omicron variant arrived in March 2022.

title.narrative: Economic policy reform and management and private sector development

description.narrative: Lao PDR: Second Private sector and SME Development Program was designed to support an enabling environment through high-impact policy reforms with capacity-building measures ‍ 1 Governor of the Bank of LaoPDR approved development and launch of a web-based credit information system. ‍ 2 Foreign Trade and Policy Department is providing trade information and guidelines to SMEs, especially women entrepreneurs. ‍ 3 Ministry of Planning and Investment established the Provincial Public–Private Dialogue Forum in Champasak through Governor’s Decree. ‍ 4 Ministry of Industry and Commerce implemented an enterprise registration system across all provinces. A Regulatory Impact Assessment unit was established, endorsed by the vice-minister. ‍ 5 Small and Medium-Sized Enterprise Promotion and Development Office drafted the SME Development Plan (2011–2015) and launched an expert network to mentor SME entrepreneurs on loan applications, enhancing access to finance. ‍ 6 Ministry of Science and Technology issued Intellectual Property Law and implementing regulations on geographical indication consistent with WTO.

Maldives: COVID-19 ADB provided technical assistance (TA) to support government (i) implement health response and socioeconomic package to the poor, women, migrant workers, elderly, differently abled/vulnerable groups, and businesses; (ii) strengthen the capacity of executing/implementing agencies to monitor and evaluate programs, and (iii) identify areas for further PFM reform. The TA helped deploy Rapid Response Teams in collaboration with local Police and Defense services. Around 150 staff were trained from implementing agencies. Around 100 doctors and 250 support staff were trained in critical care. The government provided training programs for job seekers, and additional health support to boost testing capacity.

Marshall Islands: Health Expenditure and Livelihoods Support Program helped mitigate the pandemic’s economic and social impacts. Health services were maintained while mitigation programs supported small business relief and recovery, and household welfare and incomes (unemployment benefits, distribution of food, farming supplies, fishing gear). ~25,915 people benefitted from at least one form of cash/in-kind support including (i) economic relief for at least 416 business owners and 300 taxi drivers; (ii) 10,272 children in school feeding programs; (iii) 14,280 people in neighboring islands and atolls (2,380 households received food baskets); and (iv) 647 women and girls from vulnerable households provided dignity kits

Mongolia: Agriculture and Rural Development Project advanced ADB's focus from agriculture to a comprehensive multisector food security engagement. It provided value chain investment loans and technical assistance for meat, dairy, berry, and vegetable processing; bee farming; crop seed production; and intensified farming sectors. Farm and herders’ output increased as a result of improvement to support services and access to finance. The project strengthened access to agricultural extension advice, new technologies, and market outlets through supply contract arrangements with participating enterprises. Training on basic standards and practices, provision of essential tools and equipment, and investments in extension services were also undertaken.

Mongolia: Food and Nutrition Social Welfare Program and Project - Covered by a social pension for informal sector workers (i.e., herders, self-employed, and nonwage earners), i.e., social insurance on a voluntary basis. ‍ Samoa: Health Expenditure and Livelihoods Support Program - Beneficiaries received social protection/assistance in the form of one-off special pension, special dividends from SNPF for contributors, utility subsidy, and unemployment benefits. ‍ Solomon Islands: COVID-19 Rapid Response Program - Social assistance was provided in the form of food rations, support to farmers and small- and medium-businesses, grants were granted to churches, provincial governments, school farms, etc. ‍ Vanuatu: COVID-19 Fiscal Response Program - Social assistance/protection in the form of employment support, grant support to businesses, tuition fee subsidies, support to agriculture.

title.narrative: Economic policy reform and management and private sector development

description.narrative: Republic of Marshall Islands: The program was designed to provide general budgetary support to help the RMI government finance countercyclical spending and maintain essential services and employment, particularly in health. It provided financial relief for businesses and workers and sustained social assistance programs for the vulnerable. The economic downturn resulted in a decline in tax revenues in FY2020, and a further decline in FY2021. COVID-19 grants helped RMI achieve a fiscal surplus equivalent to 4.3% of GDP in FY2020, with a smaller surplus of 1.4% estimated for FY2021. Without additional grants, fiscal deficits are projected in FY2022 and FY2023.

Tajikistan: COVID-19 Active Response and Expenditure Support Program, part of ADB’s Comprehensive Response to the COVID-19 Pandemic (CPRO), provided budget support to finance additional critical expenditures aimed at controlling the spread of COVID-19 and mitigating its immediate negative economic and social effects. Key outputs enabled by the program included establishing isolation facilities and deploying staff and equipment in hospitals nationwide for critical care and treatment. The government increased salaries of all medical staff (at least 80% of whom are women) caring for COVID-19 patients in quarantine facilities and procured personal protective equipment (PPEs) and mechanical ventilators through this program.

title.narrative: Economic policy reform and management and private sector development

description.narrative: The ADB's Trade and Supply Chain Finance Program follows a dual approach to deploy its capacity development initiatives for banks in developing member countries: It deploys significant resources to deepen knowledge of supply chain finance and promote market awareness of how this product has the potential to reduce financing gaps. Intense and targeted technical support is provided to a set of banks assessed for their capacity to build a supply chain finance offering; and it supports supply chain finance across 10 countries. Carbon tracking and disability inclusion are significant themes embedded with DFAT support.

The government of Tajikistan response program supported crisis affected female-owned MSMEs through temporary tax relief and concessional lending to help mitigate loss of income and to assist onward recovery. Tax concessions benefited 30,175 business entities, of which 13,670 (or 45.3%) were owned by women. Additionally, Sanoatsodirotbank had disbursed lending to 190 female-owned MSMEs. Supported MSMEs that benefited are mainly represented in industry, commerce, agriculture, and services. Loans are disbursed on concessional terms at 16% interest and a one-year grace period, compared to banking rates of 23.9% in the period between January and June 2021.

The services provided to victims of gender-based violence (GBV) under the SAFENET network include: ‍ 1. Police Services: Support and intervention by law enforcement for immediate protection and investigation of GBV cases. ‍2. Helplines: The 132 domestic violence hotline for immediate assistance and support. 3. Counseling: Psychological support and counseling to help survivors cope with trauma. 4. Safe Accommodation: Shelter and safe housing options for survivors needing immediate protection. 5. Legal Assistance: Help with legal matters, including representation and advice. 6. Referral Pathway: A structured pathway developed to guide the referral of cases to appropriate services, including adaptations at the provincial level to reach rural areas. 7. Emergency Phone Tree: Ensures timely communication and response among SAFENET members and stakeholders. 8. Public Awareness Campaigns: Dissemination of key messages about GBV services, self-care, and violence prevention through national radio, brochures, posters, social media, and press.

This policy-based operation was designed provide a more conducive business environment for SMEs. ‍ At program completion, at outcome level, the subprogram reported an increased share of registered SMEs owned by women. A total of 80,125 women-owned enterprises were registered with the Department of Enterprise Registry and Management (DERM) national database, which signified 48.4% of the total of registered businesses, an increase from the baseline of 43% in 2009 (target 48%). This is a result of the exposure of more women to enterprise development services and opportunities for capacity building. It is unclear how many of the enterprises are active at the time of writing of this report, however, as the outcome target was the percentage of women-owned enterprises registered, the target was met (although not by the original date of 2013).

Tonga: Nuku’alofa Urban Development Sector Project helped strengthen the policy environment for the delivery of urban services including water supply, waste collection services, and public sanitation facilities. The project successfully built capacity in urban planning and management within the Planning and Urban Management Agency of the Ministry of Lands, Survey and Natural Resources; the Tonga Water Board (TWB); and the Water Authority Limited (WAL). TWB and WAL improved their financial management and completed tariff reviews which helped raise revenues. Improvements to water supply and waste management, and overall living conditions have been dramatic, with reliability, efficiency and customer satisfaction increased.

Vanuatu. The $5.8 million project targeted 250 poor and vulnerable households headed by women, established local gardening schemes, offered advice on nutrition and diet, and provided seed grants for home-based food businesses to bolster economic independence and financial resilience. In addition, the investment helped finance prevention programs around gender-based violence, while an online awareness campaign to eliminate such violence reached around 15,000 adolescents.
